      3. Outer Measures#

      Our goal is to assign a meaningful notion of “size” to subsets of a space . The

      An additive length cannot be defined on every subset of ; a counterexample due to Vitali, later in these notes will make the obstruction precise. An outer measure is the useful first substitute. It is defined on all subsets, is built from countable coverings, and is countably subadditive: the size of a union is no greater than the sum of the sizes used to cover it.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • Verify the defining properties of an outer measure.

      • Generate an outer measure from a covering cost and determine when it extends that cost.

      • Prove that Lebesgue outer measure agrees with length and area on rectangles.

      • Explain why no translation-invariant length can be additive on every subset of .

      3.1 Outer measures#

      Denoting by the collection of subsets of a set , we would like to define a functional that has the following properties:

      • non-negative: for all ;

      • zero on the empty set: ;

      • monotone: if ;

      • infinitely subadditive: ;

      • infinitely additive on disjoint sets: if whenever .

      We will see, however, that, generally, these conditions are too strong: in many settings there are no useful functionals that satisfy all the properties above. As a first restriction, we only consider countable subadditivity and additivity, also known as -(sub)additivity.

      Even then, these conditions are generally too restrictive, which motivates us to require fewer properties, thereby leading to the notion of an outer measure.

      Definition 3.1.1 (Outer measure)#

      An outer measure on is a function with the following properties:

      1. ;

      2. monotonicity: if , then ;

      3. -subadditivity: for every sequence it holds

      The third property is called countable subadditivity or -subadditivity.

      An outer measure is defined on all subsets of , and the sets involved in the -subadditivity property need not be disjoint. For this reason we require only the inequality there. Monotonicity is an additional property; it does not follow from -subadditivity.

      The construction of the Lebesgue outer measure on described above provides a translation-invariant functional on that coincides with length on open intervals.
